sentences.nl: Welkom bij het tweede seizoen van Heb je Zin.
sentences.en: Welcome to the second season of Heb je Zin.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Welcome to the second season of Do you Feel Like it.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Welkom bij" translates to "Welcome to," where "bij" is the preposition used for places or events.  
• "Het tweede seizoen" means "the second season," using "het" as the definite article for "seizoen" (season), and "tweede" is the ordinal number for "second."  
• "Heb je Zin" literally translates to "Do you Feel Like it," where "heb" is the verb "to have," and "zin" means "desire" or "mood." It's also the title of a show or segment.

Examples:  
- "Welkom bij het feest." (Welcome to the party.)  
- "Dit is het derde boek in de serie." (This is the third book in the series.)  
- "Heb je zin om te gaan?" (Do you feel like going?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Welkom bij de opening van het nieuwe museum." (Welcome to the opening of the new museum.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Heb je zin" is a common phrase in Dutch used informally to ask if someone feels like doing something or is in the mood for something. It's a casual way to gauge interest or willingness.

sentences.nl: Terwijl Xing met Marieke en Annika zit te kletsen, is Martin buiten.
sentences.en: While Xing is sitting chatting with Marieke and Annika, Martin is outside.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• While Xing with Marieke and Annika sits to chat, is Martin outside.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Terwijl" is a conjunction meaning "while," used to indicate simultaneous actions.  
• "Zit te kletsen" uses the continuous construction "zitten te + infinitive," indicating an ongoing action (sitting and chatting).  
• Word order: In subordinate clauses introduced by "terwijl," the verb moves to the end.  

Examples:  
- Terwijl ik lees, luister ik naar muziek. (While I read, I listen to music.)  
- Hij staat te koken in de keuken. (He is standing and cooking in the kitchen.)  
- Ze ligt te slapen op de bank. (She is lying down and sleeping on the couch.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Terwijl de kinderen buiten spelen, maakt hun moeder het avondeten. (While the children play outside, their mother makes dinner.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Hij neemt afscheid van zijn vriend Lars.
sentences.en: He says goodbye to his friend Lars.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He takes farewell of his friend Lars.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Afscheid nemen van" is an idiomatic expression meaning "to say goodbye to." It uses the verb "nemen" (to take) combined with "afscheid" (farewell).  
• The verb "nemen" is in the present tense and is followed by the preposition "van" (of/from) to indicate from whom the farewell is being taken.  
• Example 1: Zij neemt afscheid van haar collega. (She says goodbye to her colleague.)  
• Example 2: Wij nemen afscheid van de zomer. (We say goodbye to the summer.)  
• Example 3: Ik neem afscheid van mijn oude huis. (I say goodbye to my old house.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij neemt afscheid van zijn familie. (He says goodbye to his family.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, saying "afscheid nemen" often involves a significant or somewhat formal goodbye, not just a casual "bye" in passing. It may indicate the end of a visit or a more permanent departure.

sentences.nl: Want Lars reist vanavond al naar Amsterdam Centraal Station.
sentences.en: Because Lars is already travelling to Amsterdam Central Station tonight.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Because Lars travels tonight already to Amsterdam Central Station.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Want" is a coordinating conjunction meaning "because" and does not change word order.  
• "Reist" is the present tense form of "reizen" (to travel).  
• "Vanavond" means "tonight," indicating a time expression often placed at the beginning or middle of a sentence.  
• "Al" means "already," signaling that something happens sooner than expected.  
• "Amsterdam Centraal Station" is a proper noun, referring to the main train station in Amsterdam.

- Ik ga morgen al naar huis. (I'm going home already tomorrow.)  
- Zij komt vanmiddag al aan. (She is arriving already this afternoon.)  
- We vertrekken vanavond laat. (We are leaving late tonight.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Omdat het regent, blijven we binnen. (Because it is raining, we are staying inside.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Amsterdam Centraal Station is one of the busiest and most important train stations in the Netherlands, serving as a major hub for both domestic and international travel.

sentences.nl: Hij heeft morgen een vroege vlucht vanaf Schiphol.
sentences.en: He has an early flight from Schiphol tomorrow.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He has tomorrow an early flight from Schiphol.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses a typical Dutch word order where the time expression "morgen" (tomorrow) comes before the direct object "een vroege vlucht" (an early flight).  
• "Vanaf" is a preposition meaning "from," indicating the starting point of the flight.  
• "Schiphol" is the name of the main international airport in the Netherlands, often used without an article.  
• Example: "Hij heeft volgende week een belangrijke vergadering." (He has an important meeting next week.)  
• Example: "Ze vertrekt over een uur vanaf het station." (She leaves in an hour from the station.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik heb overmorgen een vroege trein vanaf Utrecht Centraal. (I have an early train the day after tomorrow from Utrecht Central.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Schiphol is one of the busiest airports in Europe and is located near Amsterdam. It's a central hub for international and domestic flights, making it a familiar reference point in Dutch travel contexts.

sentences.nl: Hoe waren je twee weken? — Nou, ik heb zeker geen slechte tijd gehad.
sentences.en: How were your two weeks? — Well, I certainly didn't have a bad time.
sentences.note: geen slechte tijd: de-word, so -e even after geen. Mirror of s19.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• How were your two weeks? — Well, I have certainly no bad time had.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hoe waren je twee weken?" uses the past tense of "zijn" (to be) to ask about a period of time that has already occurred.  
• "Nou" is an interjection that can be translated as "well" and is often used to introduce a statement or response.  
• The phrase "zeker geen" means "certainly no" or "definitely not," used to emphasize a negation.  
• "Ik heb... gehad" is the present perfect tense in Dutch, combining "heb" (have) with a past participle to describe an action in the past.

Examples:  
• "Hoe was je vakantie?" (How was your vacation?)  
• "Nou, dat was zeker een avontuur." (Well, that was certainly an adventure.)  
• "Ik heb nooit zoiets gezien." (I have never seen something like that.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Hoe ging je examen? — Nou, ik heb zeker geen fouten gemaakt." (How did your exam go? — Well, I certainly made no mistakes.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to ask about someone's holiday or time off when they return, as it shows interest in their experiences and well-being.

sentences.nl: Het was een leerzame periode met veel gezellige avonden, maar ook een rustige omgeving met veel mooie natuur.
sentences.en: It was an educational period with lots of cosy evenings, but also a quiet environment with lots of beautiful nature.
sentences.note: Four adjectives, all -e: de periode, plural avonden, de omgeving, de natuur. leerzaam → leerzame (aa loses a letter).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• It was a educational period with many cozy evenings, but also a quiet environment with much beautiful nature.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het was" is the past tense of "zijn" (to be), indicating a completed action or state in the past.  
• "Leerzame" is an adjective meaning "educational," describing "periode." Adjectives in Dutch often end in -e when preceding a noun.  
• "Veel" means "many" or "much," and it is used here to describe both "gezellige avonden" (many cozy evenings) and "mooie natuur" (much beautiful nature).  
• "Gezellige" is an adjective meaning "cozy" or "pleasant," a word often used in Dutch culture to describe warm, friendly atmospheres or gatherings.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Het was een inspirerende ervaring." (It was an inspiring experience.)  
  - "We hebben veel mooie herinneringen." (We have many beautiful memories.)  
  - "De omgeving was erg rustig." (The environment was very quiet.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Het was een drukke week met veel deadlines, maar ook een kans om te leren. (It was a busy week with many deadlines, but also a chance to learn.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Gezellig" is a quintessentially Dutch concept, often used to describe a cozy, pleasant, and sociable atmosphere. It's an important part of Dutch social interactions and culture, emphasizing warmth and friendliness in gatherings and environments.

sentences.nl: Ik hou echt van het Nederlandse platteland.
sentences.en: I really love the Dutch countryside.
sentences.note: het Nederlandse platteland: het-word, definite → -e. Pairs with s30.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I hold really of the Dutch countryside.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik hou van" means "I love" or "I like," where "hou" is a colloquial form of "houden van" (to love/like).  
• "Echt" means "really" and is used for emphasis.  
• "Het Nederlandse platteland" translates to "the Dutch countryside," where "het" is the definite article, and "Nederlandse" is the adjective form of "Nederland" (Netherlands).

Examples:  
- Ik hou van honden. (I love dogs.)  
- Zij houdt echt van muziek. (She really loves music.)  
- Wij houden van het strand. (We love the beach.)

## 3. Create a New Example

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The Dutch countryside is known for its picturesque landscapes, including windmills, tulip fields, and canals, which are iconic symbols of the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Heb je veel van Drenthe gezien? — Ja, ik ben naar Orvelte geweest.
sentences.en: Did you see much of Drenthe? — Yes, I went to Orvelte.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Have you much of Drenthe seen? — Yes, I am to Orvelte been.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the perfect tense with "hebben" as an auxiliary verb for "heb je...gezien" (have you...seen) and "zijn" as an auxiliary verb for "ben...geweest" (am...been).  
• "Veel van Drenthe" (much of Drenthe) involves a partitive construction, indicating a portion of a larger whole.  
• The structure "ben naar...geweest" is common for indicating places one has visited.

Examples:  
- Heb je veel van Nederland gezien? (Have you seen much of the Netherlands?)  
- Ik ben naar Amsterdam geweest. (I have been to Amsterdam.)  
- Heb je veel van het museum gezien? (Have you seen much of the museum?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Heb je veel van de stad gezien? — Ja, ik ben naar de oude markt geweest. (Have you seen much of the city? — Yes, I have been to the old market.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Drenthe is a province in the Netherlands known for its natural landscapes and historic sites like the village of Orvelte, which is a preserved museum village showcasing traditional Dutch rural life.

sentences.nl: Dat is echt een leuk dorp.
sentences.en: That is a really nice village.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• That is really a nice village.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dat is" is a simple subject-verb construction meaning "That is."  
• "echt" means "really" and is used for emphasis.  
• "een leuk dorp" translates to "a nice village," where "leuk" is an adjective meaning "nice" or "fun," and "dorp" is "village." The adjective "leuk" precedes the noun "dorp" as is typical in Dutch.  

Examples:  
• Dit is echt een mooie stad. (This is really a beautiful city.)  
• Hij is echt een goede vriend. (He is really a good friend.)  
• Dat was echt een spannende film. (That was really an exciting movie.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ze is echt een slimme student. (She is really a smart student.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, many small villages ("dorpen") have their own unique charm and character, often with traditional architecture and local festivals.

sentences.nl: En we zijn ook uitgeweest naar een Chinees restaurant en naar een lokale bruine kroeg met goede muziek en lekker bier.

sentences.note: goede muziek (de) vs lekker bier (het, no article) — de/het decides.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And we have also gone out to a Chinese restaurant and to a local brown pub with good music and tasty beer.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En we zijn ook uitgeweest" uses the present perfect tense ("zijn uitgeweest") to describe a past action with relevance to the present. "Uitgeweest" is the past participle of "uitgaan" (to go out), and "zijn" is the auxiliary verb.  
• "Naar een Chinees restaurant" uses the preposition "naar" to indicate direction or destination.  
• "Lokale bruine kroeg" refers to a type of traditional Dutch pub, where "lokale" (local) is an adjective describing "bruine kroeg" (brown pub), a common term for cozy, traditional bars in the Netherlands.

Examples:  
• "We zijn naar de film geweest." (We have been to the movies.)  
• "Ik ben uitgeweest met mijn vrienden." (I went out with my friends.)  
• "We gaan naar een gezellig café." (We are going to a cozy café.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Gisteren zijn we naar een Italiaans restaurant geweest en daarna naar een jazzclub." (Yesterday we went to an Italian restaurant and then to a jazz club.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• A "bruine kroeg" is a traditional Dutch pub known for its cozy atmosphere, often featuring wooden interiors and dim lighting. These pubs are popular spots for socializing over drinks and are considered an integral part of Dutch social life.

sentences.nl: Mooi, ik ben blij.
sentences.en: Great, I'm glad.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Beautiful, I am happy.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "mooi" typically means "beautiful" or "nice" but can also function as an interjection, similar to "great" or "awesome" in English.  
• The sentence uses the present tense of the verb "zijn" (to be): "ben" (am).  
• Word order in Dutch is similar to English in this simple sentence: subject ("ik") followed by the verb ("ben").  
• Examples:  
  - "Mooi, laten we beginnen." (Great, let's start.)  
  - "Ik ben moe." (I am tired.)  
  - "Mooi weer vandaag." (Nice weather today.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Mooi, ik heb het gevonden." (Great, I found it.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, "mooi" as an interjection is commonly used in casual conversations to express satisfaction or approval, similar to "great" in English.

sentences.nl: Dan was het geen slecht advies om hier Nederlands te leren.

sentences.nl: Zeker Martin, ik ben je erg dankbaar.
sentences.en: Definitely, Martin, I'm very grateful to you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Certainly Martin, I am you very grateful.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zeker" is an adverb meaning "certainly" or "surely." It is often used to confirm or agree with something.  
• "Ik ben" is the present tense of "zijn" (to be) for the first person singular, meaning "I am."  
• "Je" is the informal singular form of "you" in Dutch, used as an object pronoun here.  
• "Erg" is an adverb meaning "very" and is used to intensify an adjective.  
• "Dankbaar" is an adjective meaning "grateful."

Additional Examples:  
• Ik ben je heel dankbaar. (I am very grateful to you.)  
• Hij is erg vriendelijk. (He is very friendly.)  
• Zeker, dat is een goed idee. (Certainly, that is a good idea.)

## 3. Create a New Example

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, expressing gratitude with phrases like "ik ben je dankbaar" is common and appreciated, especially in informal settings among friends and family.

sentences.nl: Hm, kun je me iets meer vertellen? — Ben je nu nog verliefd op Marieke of niet meer? — Maar Martin kan niet zeggen.
sentences.en: Hm, can you tell me a bit more? — Are you still in love with Marieke now, or not any more? — But Martin can't say.

sentences.nl: Dat heeft hij Xing beloofd.
sentences.en: He promised Xing that.
sentences.note: Inversion + participle last: Dat heeft hij … beloofd.

sentences.nl: Dus begint hij over iets anders.
sentences.en: So he starts talking about something else.

sentences.nl: Eh in oktober speelt het Nederlands elftal tegen Zweden in Stockholm.
sentences.en: Er, in October the Dutch national team plays Sweden in Stockholm.
sentences.note: het Nederlands elftal: fixed name, no -e. Compare s14.

grammarHits.explanation: A fixed term — on the slide word for word, so no -e even after het. Compare s14 'het Nederlandse platteland'.

sentences.nl: Daar wil ik heen.
sentences.en: I want to go there.

sentences.nl: Huh? — Nou ja, Lars begrijpt het.
sentences.en: Huh? — Well, Lars understands.

sentences.nl: Oké.
sentences.en: Okay.

sentences.nl: Nou, wat leuk dat je naar Zweden komt.
sentences.en: Well, how nice that you're coming to Sweden.

sentences.nl: Dan kunnen we samen gaan en je kunt bij mij blijven slapen.
sentences.en: Then we can go together and you can stay over at my place.
sentences.note: 🔴 Verb forms: kunnen … gaan, kunt … blijven slapen (two infinitives at the end).

sentences.nl: Ja, leuk.
sentences.en: Yes, great.

sentences.nl: Nou, Lars, dan wens ik je een goede reis terug.
sentences.en: Well, Lars, then I wish you a good trip back.

grammarHits.explanation: De reis: -e after een.

sentences.nl: Dankjewel.
sentences.en: Thank you.

sentences.nl: Tot oktober en veel succes met de liefde.
sentences.en: Until October, and good luck with love.

sentences.nl: Dan loopt Martin verder naar het huisje van Xing.
sentences.en: Then Martin walks on to Xing's cottage.

sentences.nl: Hey, daar is Gianluca met een bos bloemen.
sentences.en: Hey, there's Gianluca with a bunch of flowers.

sentences.nl: Hoi Gianluca, zegt Martin opgewekt.
sentences.en: Hi Gianluca, Martin says cheerfully.

grammarHits.explanation: Describes how he says it, not a noun: no -e (the slide's 'Zij schrijft mooi').

sentences.nl: Ehm, hoi Martin.
sentences.en: Um, hi Martin.

sentences.nl: Nou, Gianluca heeft een mooie bos bloemen voor Marieke gekocht.
sentences.en: Well, Gianluca has bought a beautiful bunch of flowers for Marieke.

grammarHits.explanation: De bos: -e after een.

sentences.nl: Hij weet dus nog niet dat Marieke hem eigenlijk niet leuk vindt.
sentences.en: So he doesn't know yet that Marieke doesn't actually like him.
sentences.note: 🔴 Subclause after dat: verb last — niet leuk vindt.

sentences.nl: En hij weet het nog niet van Martin en Xing.
sentences.en: And he doesn't know about Martin and Xing yet.

sentences.nl: Hij denkt waarschijnlijk nog dat Martin Marieke ook wil.
sentences.en: He probably still thinks that Martin wants Marieke too.
sentences.note: Subclause after denkt dat: ook wil at the end.

sentences.nl: Hoe gaat dat verder? — Heb je al bijvoeglijke naamwoorden in deze les gehoord? — En begrijp je waarom het bijvoeglijk naamwoord de ene keer wel op een -e eindigt en de andere keer niet? — Dat is iets wat veel mensen fout doen.
sentences.en: How will it continue? — Have you already heard adjectives in this lesson? — And do you understand why the adjective sometimes ends in -e and other times not? — That is something a lot of people get wrong.

grammarHits.explanation: Plural: -e.
A fixed grammar term: no -e even after het. In the same sentence the plural gets -e.

sentences.nl: En het is belangrijk als je goed Nederlands wilt spreken.
sentences.en: And it is important if you want to speak Dutch well.

grammarHits.explanation: Describes how you speak: no -e.

sentences.nl: Want in heel veel zinnen zit een bijvoeglijk naamwoord.
sentences.en: Because a great many sentences contain an adjective.

sentences.nl: Kijk nog eens goed naar deze lessen van #dutchgrammar als je het moeilijk vindt.
sentences.en: Take another good look at these #dutchgrammar lessons if you find it difficult.

sentences.nl: Tot de volgende keer bij Heb je Zin.
sentences.en: Until next time at Heb je Zin.

sentences.nl: Doei.
sentences.en: Bye.

mijn.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi/ is spelled as 'ij' in Dutch, which is pronounced similarly to 'ei'.
mijn.fast: In connected speech, the diphthong /ɛi/ in ‘mijn’ might be pronounced more smoothly, closer to [mɛi̯n].

bart.spelling: The 'aa' in open syllable becomes /aː/, while closed syllable shortens to /ɑ/.
bart.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in ‘bart’ can become unreleased or assimilate to a following consonant.

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

welkom.spelling: The combination 'w' and 'e' produces a /ʋɛ/ sound, common in Dutch words starting with 'wel-'.
welkom.fast: In fast speech, the final /m/ in 'welkom' can become nasalized before a following vowel.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

tweede.spelling: The 'ee' in 'tweede' is a long vowel sound /eː/ followed by a schwa /ə/ at the end.
tweede.fast: In connected speech, the initial /t/ in ‘tweede’ can become less aspirated, sounding closer to [tw].

seizoen.spelling: The 'ei' in Dutch is pronounced as /ɛi/ and the 'z' creates the /z/ sound.
seizoen.fast: In connected speech, the initial /s/ in ‘seizoen’ may be pronounced more softly or even slightly voiced, especially after a voiced sound.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

zin.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in ‘zin heb’ may be realized as a nasalized vowel or dropped in informal contexts.

dit.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ is followed by a voiceless plosive /t/, typical of closed syllables.
dit.fast: In rapid speech, the /t/ in ‘dit is’ can become a flap [ɾ] or be elided entirely.

aflevering.spelling: The prefix ‘af-’ indicates a separable prefix, showing a clear boundary with the root.
aflevering.fast: The initial /f/ of ‘aflevering’ may assimilate to a voiced [v] in connected speech, especially after voiced sounds.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

dutchgrammar.fast: In connected speech, the final /r/ in ‘grammar’ may become less pronounced or vocalized.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

gaan.spelling: The open syllable ga- carries a long /aː/ sound.
gaan.fast: In connected speech, the initial /ɣ/ in ‘gaan we’ may become more voiceless, sounding closer to [x] before a vowel.

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

xing.spelling: The letter 'x' typically represents the /ks/ sound in Dutch, followed by the short vowel /ɪ/.
xing.fast: In rapid speech, the /ks/ sound in 'xing' may be pronounced more smoothly, with less emphasis on the /k/ sound.

met.spelling: The vowel ‘e’ in ‘met’ is pronounced as a short open-mid front unrounded vowel /ɛ/.
met.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in ‘met’ may be assimilated or become a glottal stop, especially before a word starting with a vowel.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

annika.spelling: The 'a' in Annika is pronounced as /ɑ/ due to its position and stress pattern.
annika.fast: The initial /a/ can be slightly lengthened or nasalized in connected speech depending on the speaker's accent.

kletsen.spelling: The combination 'klets' uses /ɛ/ as a short vowel sound in closed syllables.
kletsen.fast: In connected speech, the /t/ in ‘kletst hij’ may be elided, resulting in a smoother transition.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

hij.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' is pronounced as /ɛi̯/, commonly found in Dutch words.
hij.fast: In connected speech, 'hij is' often reduces to /ɦɛis/ with the initial /ɦ/ sometimes dropping.

neemt.spelling: Open syllable ne- indicates long /eː/, closed neem retains the long vowel.
neemt.fast: Final /t/ in ‘neemt hij’ may become a soft [t̚] when followed by a vowel.

afscheid.spelling: The prefix 'af-' shows a consistent pronunciation with /ɑf/ across similar words.
afscheid.fast: The final /d/ in ‘afscheid nemen’ may be pronounced as a flap [ɾ] in connected speech.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

vriend.spelling: The initial cluster 'vr-' is common in Dutch, and the final '-d' is pronounced as /t/.
vriend.fast: In rapid speech, the final /t/ in 'vriend' may be less pronounced or even dropped when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

amsterdam.spelling: The initial /ɑm/ is pronounced with a short 'a', and the 'st' cluster is pronounced together.
amsterdam.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'amsterdam' might be less pronounced, blending into the following syllable.

heeft.spelling: The vowel /eː/ in heeft is long due to the closed syllable ending in -ft.
heeft.fast: In fast speech, the /t/ in ‘heeft hij’ may assimilate to the /h/ of ‘hij’.

morgen.spelling: The /r/ is pronounced with a uvular fricative /ɣ/ in the standard Dutch accent.
morgen.fast: The final /n/ may be elided in casual speech, leading to a pronunciation like [ˈmɔrɣə].

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

vroege.spelling: The 'oe' in 'vroege' represents a long /uː/ sound, common in Dutch words.
vroege.fast: In connected speech, the final /ə/ in ‘vroege’ may become a schwa [ə] or be elided before a vowel.

vlucht.spelling: The cluster 'vl' followed by 'ucht' represents the /vlʏxt/ sound with a short vowel.
vlucht.fast: In casual speech, the final /t/ in 'vlucht' may be less aspirated or even dropped before a following consonant.

vanaf.spelling: The combination 'vanaf' uses 'van-' prefix, often used in prepositions to denote direction or starting point.
vanaf.fast: In connected speech, 'vanaf' may be pronounced quickly, reducing the second syllable to a schwa sound.

hoe.spelling: The vowel sound /uː/ in 'hoe' is represented by the letters 'oe', a common Dutch spelling for this sound.
hoe.fast: In rapid speech, the /ˈɦuː/ in ‘hoe gaat’ may blend, with the /ɦ/ becoming less pronounced, sounding like /uːɣaːt/.

twee.spelling: The diphthong 'ee' in open syllables is pronounced as /eː/.
twee.fast: In connected speech, the /t/ in 'twee' may not be fully released before a following consonant.

weken.spelling: The long vowel /eː/ is represented by 'ee' in open syllables.
weken.fast: The final /k/ in ‘week ik’ may become unreleased [k̚] when followed by another word starting with a vowel.

zeker.spelling: The initial 'z' is pronounced as /z/ and the 'e' is long /eː/ in open syllables.
zeker.fast: In rapid speech, the final /r/ in 'zeker' may be realized as a tap or even omitted, blending into the following word.

was.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable indicates 'a' is pronounced as /ɑ/.
was.fast: The /s/ in ‘was hij’ may be voiced to [z] in connected speech before the voiced 'hij'.

leerzame.spelling: The combination 'ee' in 'leer' represents the long /eː/ sound in Dutch.
leerzame.fast: The final /ə/ in ‘leerzame’ can be reduced to a very short schwa [ə] or even elided in rapid speech.

periode.spelling: The 'e' at the end of 'periode' is pronounced as /ə/, a schwa sound commonly used in unstressed syllables.
periode.fast: In connected speech, the final /ə/ in 'periode' may be reduced further or elided, especially in fast speech.

veel.spelling: The vowel 'ee' in a closed syllable is pronounced as the long vowel /eː/.
veel.fast: In connected speech, the final /l/ in 'veel' may become a dark [ɫ], especially before a consonant.

gezellige.spelling: The /ɣ/ sound is typical for 'g' in Dutch, and the double 'l' indicates a short vowel sound before it.
gezellige.fast: In connected speech, the /ɣ/ at the start of 'gezellige' might be softened to a more /x/-like sound depending on regional accents.

avonden.spelling: The 'avond' shows an open syllable with long /aː/, which is maintained in the plural form.
avonden.fast: In connected speech, the final /n/ in ‘avonden’ may be weakened or elided, especially in casual conversation.

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

rustige.spelling: The 'ui' in 'rustige' represents the diphthong /œy/, which is often spelled with 'ui' in Dutch.
rustige.fast: In connected speech, the final /ə/ in ‘rustige’ may be reduced or even elided, particularly in fast or informal contexts.

omgeving.spelling: The prefix om- is unstressed, while -geving has primary stress with a long /eː/ due to the open syllable.
omgeving.fast: In connected speech, the final /ŋ/ in 'omgeving' may be realized as a more palatalized [ŋj] before front vowels.

mooie.spelling: The 'oo' in an open syllable indicates a long /oː/ sound.
mooie.fast: In connected speech, the final /ə/ in 'mooie' might be less distinct, merging into a preceding or following vowel.

natuur.spelling: The vowel sound /aː/ is long due to the open syllable structure, and /yːr/ is long due to the final 'r'.
natuur.fast: In connected speech, the final /r/ in 'natuur' may be pronounced more softly or even dropped, especially in casual conversation.

gezien.spelling: Long vowel /iː/ in open syllable ‘zie’ remains long in ‘gezien’.
gezien.fast: In connected speech, the final /n/ in ‘gezien ik’ might be elided, resulting in a nasalized vowel [ɣəˈziː].

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

leuk.spelling: The diphthong 'eu' in Dutch generally corresponds to the sound /øː/ or /œy/.
leuk.fast: In fast speech, the final /k/ in 'leuk' may be unreleased or assimilate to the following sound.

uitgeweest.spelling: The prefix 'uit' indicates a completed action, similar to 'out' in English.
uitgeweest.fast: In connected speech, the /t/ in ‘uit’ may assimilate or be dropped before a voiced consonant.

chinees.spelling: The 'ch' in 'chinees' represents the /ʃ/ sound, which is uncommon in Dutch and borrowed from French.
chinees.fast: In connected speech, the /ʃ/ sound in 'chinees' may become softer before a vowel, resembling a /s/ sound.

restaurant.spelling: The initial syllable 'res-' is stressed with a short /ɛ/, and the final '-ant' is unstressed.
restaurant.fast: The final /t/ in ‘restaurant’ may be pronounced more softly or even omitted in fast, connected speech.

lokale.spelling: The 'o' in 'lo-' is long /oː/ due to open syllable, while '-ka-' is stressed with a long /aː/.
lokale.fast: The final /ə/ in 'lokale' may be reduced to a schwa or elided in fast speech, especially before a vowel.

bruine.spelling: The diphthong /œy̯/ is represented by the spelling 'ui'.
bruine.fast: The final schwa /ə/ in ‘bruine’ may be reduced to a very short vowel or even elided in fast, connected speech.

kroeg.spelling: The long /uː/ in the open syllable 'kroeg' is represented by 'oe'.
kroeg.fast: The /x/ at the end of 'kroeg' may be softened to a [ɣ] in casual speech.

goede.spelling: The 'oe' in 'goede' represents the long /uː/ sound.
goede.fast: The final /ə/ in ‘goede’ may be reduced to a schwa or even omitted in rapid speech, blending into the following word.

muziek.spelling: The 'ie' in 'muziek' indicates a long /iː/ sound, typical for Dutch words with 'ie'.
muziek.fast: In rapid speech, final /k/ in 'muziek is' might be unreleased or assimilated to [k̚] before the vowel.

lekker.spelling: The short /ɛ/ sound is represented by 'e' in a closed syllable.
lekker.fast: In fast speech, the second syllable may reduce to a schwa, sounding like [ˈlɛkə].

bier.spelling: The vowel 'ie' represents the long vowel /iː/.
bier.fast: In rapid speech, the final /r/ in 'bier' may be realized as a tap or even omitted before a vowel.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
dan.fast: In rapid speech, 'dan ik' may have the /n/ assimilated to [ŋ] before a velar sound.

advies.spelling: The 'd' in 'advies' is pronounced /d/ at the start of the word, and the 'v' is pronounced as /v/.
advies.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in 'advies' may be softened or elided before a following vowel.

erg.spelling: The 'g' in 'erg' is pronounced as a voiced velar fricative /ɣ/.
erg.fast: In fast speech, the final /ɣ/ in 'erg' may become less voiced or assimilate to a /k/ when followed by a voiceless consonant.

dankbaar.spelling: The combination 'nk' produces a nasal sound, and the open syllable 'baar' has a long vowel /aːr/.
dankbaar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘dankbaar’ can become a tap or even silent in casual speech, especially before a consonant.

jou.spelling: The diphthong /ɑu/ in 'jou' is a common Dutch sound found in many words.
jou.fast: In rapid speech, 'jou' can merge with preceding or following words, causing the /j/ to become more like a [ʝ] or even be elided altogether.

bent.spelling: Closed syllable with short vowel /ɛ/ in bent.
bent.fast: In fast speech, final /t/ in ‘bent’ may become a flap [ɾ] before a vowel, as in ‘bent u’.

vrolijk.spelling: The combination 'oo' in an open syllable indicates a long /oː/ vowel.
vrolijk.fast: The final /k/ may be devoiced and become more of a [x] sound in connected speech.

maan.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ is indicated by the doubled 'aa' in an open syllable, followed by a nasal /n/.
maan.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ in ‘maan’ may become more nasalized or even drop before a consonant, as in ‘de maan schijnt’.

gekeken.spelling: Diphthong /ɛi/ in kijk creates the long vowel sound.
gekeken.fast: The final /k/ in ‘kijk ik’ may be unreleased [k̚] or assimilated to a glottal stop before a following vowel.

nee.spelling: The long vowel /eː/ is represented by the single vowel 'e' in an open syllable.
nee.fast: In rapid speech, ‘nee’ may be pronounced more quickly, reducing the length of the vowel.

beetje.spelling: The 'ee' in 'beet' represents a long /eː/ sound, and the 'tje' ending indicates a diminutive form.
beetje.fast: In connected speech, the final /ə/ in 'beetje' may be less pronounced or assimilated depending on the following word.

ingewikkeld.spelling: The prefix 'in-' indicates a state of being, and 'gewikkeld' comes from 'wikkelen' meaning to wrap, creating a sense of complexity.
ingewikkeld.fast: In rapid speech, the 't' at the end of 'ingewikkeld' may be unreleased or assimilated into the following word, especially if it starts with a consonant.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

verliefd.spelling: The prefix 'ver-' is unstressed, and the vowel 'ie' in the stressed syllable is pronounced as /iː/.
verliefd.fast: The final /d/ in ‘verliefd op’ may become unreleased [d̚] or assimilate to [t] before voiceless consonants.

niet.spelling: The vowel 'ie' is pronounced as a long /iː/ sound.
niet.fast: In casual speech, the /t/ in 'niet' may become unreleased or assimilate to a following consonant.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

kan.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is typical in closed syllables like 'kan'.
kan.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in 'kan' may be unreleased or nasalized before a following consonant.

zeggen.spelling: The ‘z’ at the start is pronounced /z/, a voiced sound, typical for words starting with ‘z’ in Dutch.
zeggen.fast: In rapid speech, the final /n/ in ‘zeggen we’ may become nasalized and blend into the following word.

beloofd.spelling: Open syllable be- indicates unstressed schwa /ə/, closed -loofd indicates long /oː/.
beloofd.fast: In rapid speech, the final /d/ in ‘beloofd’ may assimilate to a voiced [t] before a voiceless consonant.

dus.spelling: The vowel 'u' in 'dus' is pronounced as the short /ʏ/ sound, common in closed syllables.
dus.fast: The /s/ in ‘dus ik’ can be pronounced as a slightly longer [sː] due to assimilation with the following vowel.

wil.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ in wil closes with the liquid /l/.
wil.fast: In fast speech, ‘wil ik’ may blend, reducing the /l/ to a lighter touch before the vowel.

kunnen.spelling: The 'u' in 'kunnen' is pronounced as a short /ʏ/, typical for closed syllables.
kunnen.fast: In connected speech, the final /n/ in 'kun je' might be elided, resulting in /kʏ jə/.

mij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch pronouns, giving a distinct sound.
mij.fast: The word 'mij' may become reduced to a schwa [mə] in fast, connected speech.

tot.spelling: The word 'tot' follows the closed syllable pattern, resulting in a short vowel sound /ɔ/.
tot.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'tot' may become less aspirated or even assimilate with a following consonant.

liefde.spelling: The ie in liefde is pronounced as a long /iː/, typical for Dutch vowel combinations.
liefde.fast: The final /də/ in ‘liefde’ may reduce to a schwa sound in rapid speech, particularly when followed by another vowel.

verder.spelling: The 'er' ending is pronounced /ər/, a common pattern in Dutch adjectives.
verder.fast: In casual speech, the /r/ at the end of ‘verder’ may be softer or even drop out, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ˈvɛdə].

huisje.spelling: The 'ui' diphthong in Dutch is pronounced /œy̯/, and 'je' indicates a diminutive form, pronounced /jə/.
huisje.fast: In rapid speech, the /j/ in 'huisje' might assimilate slightly to a softer sound depending on the preceding word, linking smoothly into the next vowel.

voor.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ in 'voor' is due to the open syllable, which is typical in Dutch pronunciation patterns.
voor.fast: In connected speech, the /r/ in 'voor' may be pronounced as a tap [ɾ] or even elided entirely, depending on the speaker and regional accent.

weet.spelling: Open syllable we- indicates a long /eː/ sound.
weet.fast: In rapid speech, final /t/ in ‘weet ik’ may become a glottal stop [ʔ] before a vowel.

vindt.spelling: Short /ɪ/ in closed syllable vin- indicates the short vowel sound.
vindt.fast: The final /t/ in ‘vindt hij’ can assimilate to a glottal stop [ʔ] before a vowel.

denkt.spelling: The 'nk' in 'denk' represents a nasal sound, often pronounced with a more nasal quality.
denkt.fast: In fast speech, the 't' in ‘denkt hij’ may assimilate and be pronounced like a softer [d] sound.

gaat.spelling: The long /aː/ in 'gaat' is due to the open syllable and doubling of the vowel.
gaat.fast: In fast speech, the final /t/ in 'gaat hij' may be softened or omitted before the following /h/.

waarom.spelling: The open syllable ‘wa-’ shows a long /aː/ sound, while ‘-rom’ has a short /ɔ/.
waarom.fast: In fast speech, the final /m/ in ‘waarom ik’ can assimilate with a following vowel, sometimes sounding like [ʋaːˈrɔmɪk].

keer.spelling: The long vowel /eː/ is indicated by the 'ee' spelling in a closed syllable.
keer.fast: The final /r/ in ‘keer ik’ may become less distinct or vocalized in connected speech.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

doen.spelling: The spelling ‘oe’ consistently represents the long /u/ sound.
doen.fast: In fast speech, final /n/ in ‘doen’ often becomes nasalized or drops before a vowel, as in ‘doe ik’.

als.spelling: In Dutch, 'al' is pronounced with a short /ɑ/ sound, and 's' retains its /s/ sound.
als.fast: In connected speech, the /s/ in 'als' can become voiced to [z] when followed by a voiced consonant.

goed.spelling: Dutch /ɣ/ at the onset is a voiced velar fricative, typical in words beginning with 'g'.
goed.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'goed' can be unreleased or assimilate, especially before a vowel.

spreken.spelling: Open syllable spre- shows long /eː/, closed sprak changes vowel to /a/.
spreken.fast: Final /k/ in ‘spreek ik’ often assimilates to an unreleased [k̚] before the following vowel.

volgende.spelling: The 'volg-' root in 'volgende' maintains a short /ɔ/ due to the following consonant, despite the open syllable.
volgende.fast: In rapid speech, the 'd' in 'volgende' can be elided, making the pronunciation closer to /ˈvɔl.xə.nə/.

source.title: Grammar 2 les 17 — adjectives: when there is no extra -e (review of Grammar 1 les 9 + 10)

rules.name: adjective + -e
rules.how: An adjective in front of a noun gets -e: with every de-word, with het-words after de/het/dit/dat/mijn…, and in the plural.

rules.name: indefinite het-word: no -e
rules.how: A singular het-word that is indefinite keeps the adjective bare — after een, and also after geen, welk, elk, ieder.

rules.name: not before a noun: no -e
rules.how: After zijn/worden/vinden, or describing how someone does something, the adjective never gets -e.
examples: before a noun vs describing the verb

rules.name: spelling when -e is added
rules.how: Adding -e opens the syllable, so the spelling adjusts: short vowel doubles the consonant, a double long vowel loses a letter, f→v, s→z; -ig and diphthongs don't change.

rules.name: fixed combinations: no -e
rules.how: Some adjective + het-word pairs are fixed terms and never take -e, even after het. Bart's advice on the slide: no need to learn them — just recognise them.

rules.name: uncountable het-word: no -e
rules.how: An uncountable het-word (water, bier, geld) with no article — or after veel, meer, weinig, minder — is indefinite, so no -e. Uncountable de-words still get -e.
